rows.label: Concept
rows.text: On a flat curve friction alone must supply $F_c$, limiting speed to $v = \sqrt{\mu rg}$. **Banking** the road lets the normal force help: vertical equilibrium $N\cos\theta = mg$ and horizontal centripetal $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$ divide to give $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$ — the design angle at which no friction is needed (NEB 2024, 5m). For r = 100 m at 20 m/s with g = 10 m/s², $\tan\theta = 0.4$ and $\theta = 21.8°$.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Flat road: v_max = √(μrg) - Banked (frictionless): tan θ = v²/rg; v = √(rg tan θ) - Banked with friction: v_max = √[rg(μ + tan θ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Ideal Banking (No Friction):** At the design speed $v_0 = \sqrt{gR an heta}$, the normal reaction alone provides the centripetal force. No friction is required, so the car can negotiate the curve even on a perfectly frictionless surface.  ·  **Friction Range (Real Roads):** For speeds $v eq v_0$, static friction acts up or down the incline to prevent sliding. The safe speed range without skidding is bounded by $v_{max} = \sqrt{gR rac{ an heta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s an heta}}$ and $v_{min} = \sqrt{gR rac{ an heta - \mu_s}{1 + \mu_s an heta}}$ (valid only if denominator > 0).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The design speed is the speed at which no friction is required — the most important concept.  ·  Always check: if v²/(rg) > tan θ, the vehicle needs additional friction downward (going too fast).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **N cos θ is vertical, N sin θ is horizontal** — the angle θ is measured from the vertical, so cos pairs with mg.  ·  **Banking doesn't remove friction** — it removes the *need* for friction only at the design speed v = √(rg tan θ).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive tan θ = v²/(rg) by resolving the normal force.  ·  Solve 5 problems finding design speed from banking angle and radius.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "tan θ = v²/(rg) — compute the ratio, then tan⁻¹."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Derivation + numerical (5m): Derive tan θ = v²/rg and find θ for r = 50 m at 15 m/s (g = 9.8).** — Vertical: N cos θ = mg. Horizontal: N sin θ = mv²/r. Dividing: tan θ = v²/rg = 225/(50×9.8) = 0.459 → θ = 24.7°.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The 5m banking derivation:** N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r → tan θ = v²/rg (NEB 2024).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$ (frictionless design speed).  ·  Flat road: $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu rg}$; banked with friction: $v_{max} = \sqrt{rg(\mu + \tan\theta)/(1 - \mu\tan\theta)}$.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Railway curves are superelevated (outer rail raised) by the same tan θ = v²/rg rule.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Roads That Lean Into Turns A car rounding a flat curve relies entirely on friction — fragile at speed. Bank the road, tilt the surface inward, and the normal force itself supplies most of the centripetal force. The same physics explains why cyclists lean and why railway tracks are superelevated.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Flat (unbanked) road Friction alone supplies the centripetal force: $f = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, with $f \le \mu N = \mu mg$. Maximum safe speed: $$v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu r g}$$ ### 2.2 Banked road — derivation of the banking angle (NEB 2024) For a road banked at angle $\theta$ (frictionless ideal case), forces on the car: weight $mg$ down, normal…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 24:** banking is centripetal force engineering — the normal force's horizontal component replaces friction. - **To Conical pendulum (Topic 25):** identical geometry: $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$ appears in both. - **To Friction (Unit 4):** the flat-road limit $v = \sqrt{\mu rg}$.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **No-Friction Limit Check:** If $\mu_s = 0$, the formulas reduce exactly to $v = \sqrt{gR an heta}$. If $ an heta > 1/\mu_s$, the denominator for $v_{max}$ becomes negative, implying no upper speed limit (the car cannot slide up regardless of speed).  ·  The formula v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)] requires μ tan θ < 1 for physical validity.  ·  Railway superelevation problems: h = w tan θ where w is the standard gauge (1.5 m in Nepal).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB frequently asks: 'Why are roads banked?' — answer: to reduce friction dependence and prevent skidding.  ·  Verified PYQ: banking derivation + numerical (2024, 5m).  ·  "At the design speed, the horizontal component of the normal force supplies the entire centripetal force."
